newsitem.title: ESTONIA: ANALYSIS-Estonian bourse overcoming risk fears.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS-Estonian bourse overcoming risk fears.

text.p: Investment interest in Estonian shares is broadening, with European investors joining British and U.S. funds on the Tallinn bourse, shedding fears that the market is too risky, analysts say.
What is more, the focus is widening from just banking stocks, analysts say.
With political and macro-economic worries subsiding, confidence about investing in Estonia and its Baltic neighbours, Latvia and Lithuania, is on the rise.
"People want an exposure on the so far positive side of economic development," said Nomura's London-based Claus Mansfeldt, associate director of emerging markets in investment banking.
"We are finally seeing some interest from Scandinavia and European money is coming in."
Estonia's bourse has seen rapid growth since early 1996, outpacing its neighbours, although expansion has been reined in by fears of economic and political instability.
Despite the rise in foreign interest, figures from the Tallinn Stock Exchange show that 60 percent of total investments in 1996 came from Estonians.

Tallinn Stock Exchange spokeswoman Helo Meigas said the bourse's index, which was established last May at 100, rose to 160 by the end of December when market capitalisation was US$800 million. It now stands at 213.
Analysts said the banking sector remained the focus on Estonia's bourse, partly because of a lack of alternatives.
Trader Kari Salonen from Williams de Broe in Helsinki said he was seeing considerable interest from Britain and central Europe in Estonian banking shares which were performing well.
"Estonian banks are looking like a good buy at the moment, and we are particularly interested in the top three (Hansapank, Forekspank, and the Savings bank)," Salonen told Reuters.
"I think the bank shares could rise quite a bit this year. But Estonia is really lacking any new companies."
"So far there have not been that many pure corporates providing the necessary exposure...so people have had to invest mainly in the banks," Mansfeldt said.
"But there will be change this year and next when private sector corporates as well as the government do some substantial privatisations."
Mansfeldt said the industrial and transportation sectors in Estonia were of particular interest.
Other companies of interest were confectionery group Kalev, car seatbelt maker Norma and Sako breweries.
"I expect we'll see a reweighting of the balance on the exchange towards more industrial, transport-related companies," he said.
Analysts said several key events in 1996 had fuelled interest in Estonia and other Baltic bourses and forecast greater overseas participation.
These events included Vilniaus Bank's GDR issue and international share issues by Estonia's Savings bank and Lithuania's Birzai Milk.
"These deals are not plentiful or very large in size but they still have great novelty value," Mansfeldt said.
"I think there will be a lot of additional interest from Europe -- from Germany, Holland, Switzerland, Austria and Poland -- over the next year or two."
Elina Timonen from Merita Bank also saw wider interest.
"Interest has increased especially from central Europe, from Germany in particular," she said.
